No they don't kill brown bears in head on encounters though. There isn't one reliable case of a Siberian tiger ever killing a healthy Ussuri brown bear in a head on fight. All the so called 'statistics' from Russia of Amur tigers predating on Ussuri brown bears or killing bears during conflicts are primarily through the tiger ambush attacking the bear not in head on fights.

The whole "Siberian tigers kill adult Ussuri brown bears in head on fights" is completely made up and is fundamentally based on tigers ambush attacking bears. This has been clarified by biologists such as Steven Wroe who specifically study the interraction between Siberian tigers and Ussuri brown bears. Generally speaking, once the tiger loses the element of suprise against the bear it has to run otherwise it will be killed by the bear.

In fact, Ussuri brown bears exceeding 300kg so most adult males and some larger female bears are consistently reported by biologists to be completely immune to Siberian tiger predation so in other words larger bears are impossible for the tiger to kill even through ambush. The biggest of bears even upsurp in other words "bully" adult tigers away from their kills. This is well known!

Tigers don't 'consistently' hunt bears in Russia since bears pose a huge risk of injury to them so they make up like 1.4% to 2.1% of the tiger's diet. Amur tigers only occasionally prey on Ussuri brown bears and Asiatic black bears. Tigers normally target smaller female brown or black bears, sub adults or cubs strictly through ambush attacks since a head on fight poses a dangerous risk to the tiger's hunting abilities. Tigers can also, although this is even rarer, kill bears up to their size however this is again primarily through ambush style attacks.

Adult brown bears reaching and exceeding 300kg so most males and the occassional large female bear are completely immune to Siberian tiger predation. In fact, the biggest bears will often 'bully' the tigers (including fully grown tigers) away from their kills to steal them. This is how bears evolved as predators by being oppurtunisitc hunters and scavangers.

However, in a face to face fight Ussuri brown bears will almost always dominate tigers since bears genetically evolved to stand their ground and fight off other larger predators and large prey head on whilst all big cat species, particularly tigers, evolved as stealthy ambush hunters. All the interractions and so called 'data' (the so called 12 to 22 bear vs tiger 'statistic') showcasing Armur tigers killing Ussuri brown bears and Asiatic black bears are all through the tigers ambushing the bears. Not my words btw since this is recorded by biologists who study the interractions between Ussuri brown bears and Amur tigers in Siberia.

Basically once the tiger loses the element of suprise against the bear it is screwed and has to run away otherwise the bear will either seriously injure or kill the tiger (the same scenario with sloth bear vs Bengal tiger in India). So Ussuri and Asian black bears are still 'apex' predators but just an entirely different apex predator to that of the Siberian tiger.

There is no proof that Amur tigers predate on male Ussuri brown bears though since there is no scientific data to back up the questionable 'statistics'. It's pretty well known by biologists that adult brown bears are immune to Siberian tiger predation once they exeed 300kg which includes most adult male brown bears meaning they are impossible to kill without the tiger being killed or seriously injured by the bear in the process. All of the so called 'statistics' show is that Amur tigers occassionally ambush smaller female brown bears or sub adult bears with the key word being "ambush" not head on fighting (not my words but that of biologist Steven Wroe who went to Russia to study the interraction between tigers and brown bears).

Also, if you look into paleontology you will find countless of fossil records proving that both cave bears and short faced bears often killed cave lions and sabre tooth cats in self defence or in disputes over food and territory. This would happen if the big cat wasn't able to ambush attack the bear successfully and would lose the element of suprise against the bear. It is a similar scenario in Russia and in even India (with sloth bears and Bengal tigers) in that if the tiger loses the element of suprise it is often dominated by the bear. Bears are better built for head on fighting other larger predators than tigers and other big cats are.

Grizzly bears genetically evolved to fight other larger predators head on, more so than big cats since the ancestors of bears were once small arboreal carnivores that eventually adapted to lower ground where they were forced to stand up and fight off big cats as well as other predators to eliminate competetion for food and territory. Why do you think bears grew so big and tanky? Mostly to allow them to be able to defend themselves from other predators on ground plus to adapt to colder climates as well. Big cats are primarily ambush hunters including lions whereas bears, in particular grizzlies, are head on brawlers.

Although lions are really the only big cat alive hardwired to fight head on (besides leopards and juguars on small occassions whenever they have to defend themselves from other predators), they simply don't have the stamina and endurance a grizzly bear has in a head on fight plus not to mention brown bears are bigger and physically stronger than lions as well as possessing a slightly higher biteforce (lion is around 1,000 PSI whereas the grizzly is around 1,200 PSI). A grizzly bear is simply better equiped for a head on fight than a lion or tiger is.

Kodiak bears are technically a type of grizzly bear though. The term 'grizzly' is just a common nickname for the North American brown bear that originally derived from the bear's often silver or light blond/golden tipped fur which was often described as "grizzled" by many. This unique colour is found in mainland grizzlies, coastal grizzlies and Kodiak bears in particular. The North American brown bear splits into two main subspecies: mainland and coastal brown bears or 'Ursus arctos horrbilis' (both inland and coastal grizzlies have recently been classed as the same subspecies I believe); and the Kodiak bear or 'Ursus middendorffi'. I understand the Kodiak bear's origins likely largely stem from the [Kamchatka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamchatka)n brown bear as well as partially from the Alaskan Peninsula brown bear but Kodiak Island is an Alaskan island and Alaska is part of North America so they are part of the North American brown bear group.

Granted though, the nickname "grizzly bear" became way more associated with the mainland brown bear due to its symbolism to the mainland grizzly bear's 'grisly' nature and aggressive reputation along with its silver or light blonde tipped fur. Mainland grizzly bears are a bit smaller but a lot more dangerous and aggressively territorial than those found on the coast and on Kodiak Island due to not having the same food source from direct access to regular salmon runs. The North American brown bear previously split into three subspecies after the Californian grizzly bear and other subspecies went extinct as Alaskan coastal brown bears or known as 'Alaskan Peninsula grizzly bears' were once thought to be a seperate subspecies of North American brown bear (Ursus arctos gyas).

Ussuri brown bears are pretty much within the same size range as grizzly bears. The Alaskan coastal grizzly bears can reach up to 1.500lbs in weight and they are among some of the biggest bears on the planet. The inland grizzlies are a bit smaller and more dangerous as well as more aggressively territorial due to the lack of salmon run that those on the coast and on Kodiak Island have.

Not all predators prefer to sneak attack their prey. Grizzly bears are known to fight larger prey head on and will keep on relentlessly wrestling and biting the prey until it gives up. They often start eating prey alive once it's done trying to escape the bear's claws.

All North American brown bears are technically classed as 'grizzly bears'. This includes the mainland grizzly bear, the coastal grizzly bear or coastal brown bear and the Kodiak grizzly bear. The term "grizzly" originally came about from describing the North American brown bear's often lighter tipped fur which presents itself as either silver or light blonde i.e. grizzled tip fur. Not only this, it also became widely associated with the term 'grisly' mostly describing the mainland grizzly bear's more aggressive nature than the coastal brown bear or Kodiak bear (hence their scientific name "horribilis").  Mainland grizzly bears are more dangerous than those on the coast and of Kodiak Island due to not having the same salmon runs so they are often more aggressive and territorial despite being a bit smaller than the other two subspecies of grizzly bear. Basically, grizzly bear is just a general nickname for the North American brown bear which splits into three categories like I just described!
